title: Why so many Brazilians distrust their supreme court
text:
Why so many Brazilians distrust their supreme court
Loading...
| Rio de Janeiro
From sweeping corruption scandals across Latin America in the 2010s to recent attacks on democracy, Brazil has stood out in the region as quick to take legal action to try to hold wrongdoers to account – often at the hands of its 11-member supreme court.
But Brazil’s top court is now facing a credibility crisis, just weeks before a closely fought presidential election. Rival judges André Mendonça and Alexandre de Moraes have recently been trading tit-for-tat rulings, reigniting accusations of judicial activism and prompting concerns that the court’s turmoil could spill into the broader democratic process.
When Brazilians go to the polls Oct. 4, they’ll choose between current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who are neck-and-neck in polling. The public sees the court’s infighting as a proxy for the political face-off.
Why We Wrote This
Two supreme court justices in Brazil are trading barbs – and allegations of illegal activity. The episode underscores the broader deterioration of public faith in the institution.
Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, appointed Justice Mendonça to the court in 2021, while Justice Moraes is considered the former president’s nemesis. Mr. Moraes oversaw the trial that sentenced Jair Bolsonaro to prison last year for attempting a coup against Mr. Lula after losing the 2022 election.
The court has earned international plaudits for safeguarding democracy, but its increasingly political role has also prompted unease as individual justices – including Mr. Moraes – are seen as wielding outsize power. The infighting and allegations of improper conduct over the past two weeks now risk discrediting the court further amid widespread voter disillusionment with the political class.
“After the attempted coup, the dominant discourse outside of bolsonarista circles was that institutions were working,” says Mariana Chaise, a professor of political science at the State University of Campinas. That belief is now severely shaken, she says.
Playing gotcha?
At the root of the current turmoil is a Sept. 1 decision by Justice Mendonça to unseal police documents containing messages reportedly sent to Justice Moraes by Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced banker. Mr. Vorcaro, who has been behind bars since March, is at the center of an investigation into a $2 billion banking fraud and an influence-peddling scandal that has implicated politicians, judges, and state officials across Brazil’s ideological spectrum.
The messages show Mr. Vorcaro seeking advice from Justice Moraes in the days leading up to his first arrest in November 2025. Earlier revelations showed the judge’s wife had a multimillion-dollar contract to provide legal services to Mr. Vorcaro’s bank, the now-liquidated Banco Master.
Justice Mendonça asked the country’s top prosecutor to investigate his colleague, and Mr. Moraes retaliated with an investigation request of his own. He accused Justice Mendonça of bias in his role overseeing politically sensitive proceedings, including the Banco Master case.
Justice Mendonça then removed the director of the federal police and the agency’s intelligence chief, accusing them of illegally monitoring him to produce reports used by Justice Moraes. This was reversed by yet another justice, Lula appointee Flávio Dino, in what increasingly appears to be a politicized blow-for-blow.
The court’s top justice stepped in on Sept. 9, overruling his colleagues’ recent decisions, suspending all investigations into members of the court, and scheduling a plenary session for Sept. 15 to analyze the police report regarding Mr. Vorcaro’s relationship with Justice Moraes. This could result in further investigations – or in the report being annulled.
Distrust in the supreme court
The allegations against Justice Moraes and what some analysts see as both judges’ lack of respect for procedure are “extremely serious,” says Luiz Fernando Esteves, a law professor at the Insper business school in Sao Paulo.
The steady accumulation of justices’ individual powers over the past decade is central to the court’s current instability, he says. Recent presidents’ tendency to favor “personal affinity” over less partisan criteria in their high-court appointments has corroded the institution’s legitimacy, he says.
A Sept. 9 survey conducted by pollster Meio/Ideia found 52% of Brazilians agree that the supreme court’s judges put their personal interests ahead of the law, while just 11% disagree. Distrust in the court is high among voters on both sides of the political spectrum, a shift from a year ago when Lula supporters tended to trust the court.
“This scandal has made it difficult to imagine that these justices are acting impartially, and that they are simply applying the law – which should be a court’s most basic job,” says Dr. Esteves.
Future risk
Because polarization is already so entrenched across Brazil, this crisis is unlikely to move the needle on the election outcome, says Dr. Chaise, the political science professor.
Sen. Bolsonaro is standing in for his father in this election after the former president was barred from holding office. Polls say the race will be too close to call, and that an Oct. 25 runoff is likely.
At an Independence Day rally on Sept. 7, Sen. Bolsonaro leaned into the current judicial crisis, trying to tarnish his electoral rival by association. “A vote for Lula is a vote for Alexandre de Moraes,” he told supporters gathered in Sao Paulo, holding signs calling for the judge’s impeachment and waving blow-up dolls of President Lula in jail garb.
Mr. Lula’s backers, meanwhile, suspect Justice Mendonça of acting to benefit Sen. Bolsonaro, who has also been entangled in the Banco Master scandal. Mr. Vorcaro, the imprisoned banker, financed a biopic on the former President Bolsonaro to the tune of at least $10 million at Sen. Bolsonaro’s personal request.
On Sept. 9, Mr. Lula called for the entire investigation to be made public, to avoid selective leaks “that impact the electoral process.” The next night, at the chief justice's request, Justice Mendonça unsealed part of the Banco Master investigation.
Dr. Chaise fears, however, that the top court’s loss of credibility could ricochet onto other institutions such as the electoral court, which is responsible for guaranteeing the integrity of elections.
“There is a risk for the legitimacy of any future decision” made by these institutions, she says.
